analysis.one_liner: Makes emergency price gouging on essentials illegal and enforceable by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill to outlaw price gouging during disasters never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to charge unconscionably excessive prices for essential goods and services — including gasoline, heating fuel, water, and medical supplies — during or in anticipation of a disaster, pandemic, or declared state of emergency [S3]. It defines an illegal price as a gross disparity from the normal pre-emergency price, and lets the Federal Trade Commission enforce it the same way it enforces consumer protection rules, with penalties under the FTC Act [S3]. It also directs the FTC to set up a hotline and online portal so the public can report gouging complaints, active during and for 120 days after an emergency [S3]. The bill expressly does not override any stronger state anti-gouging laws [S3]. It was introduced on November 10, 2022 — two days after the midterm election, in the final weeks of the Congress — and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who need fuel, housing supplies, food, medicine, or medical services during a hurricane, wildfire, pandemic, or other emergency. Instead of paying a grossly inflated price when they have no alternative, they could report gouging to a federal hotline and the FTC could bring enforcement cases with civil penalties. Every state already has some residents exposed to this — the federal law would cover the gap where state laws are weak or a gouger sells across state lines.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell or offer an essential good or service at an unconscionably excessive price during, or in anticipation of, a natural disaster, pandemic, or state of emergency [S3].

Enforces the ban through the FTC with the same penalties and powers as other consumer protection violations, and extends FTC jurisdiction to common carriers and nonprofit organizations for this purpose [S3].
Directs the FTC to create a telephone hotline and online portal for the public to report price gouging complaints, operational during an emergency and for 120 days afterward [S3].
Leaves state anti-gouging laws fully intact, so consumers keep whatever protections their states already provide [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essential goods and services — fuel wholesalers and retailers, grocery and hardware chains, online marketplace sellers, hotels, and medical suppliers — who would face FTC enforcement and civil penalties if they raise prices far above pre-emergency levels during a declared emergency. Honest sellers who keep prices near normal levels would pay nothing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers and fuel sellers who gouge

drawbacks.text: The standard is vague: 'unconscionably excessive' is defined only as a gross disparity from the ordinary pre-emergency price, with no allowance spelled out for genuine cost increases, so sellers facing real supply disruptions could face enforcement for raising prices to cover higher wholesale costs [S3].

A federal ban on price spikes could discourage some sellers from stocking up or rushing extra supply into a disaster zone, if higher prices are the normal market signal for doing so; the bill contains no safe harbor for demonstrated cost increases [S3].

It duplicates protections in most states — many states already ban price gouging during emergencies — so the added benefit is mainly for consumers in states with weak laws and for sales that cross state lines [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households, the benefit is real and immediate: people fleeing a hurricane or heating their home in a fuel-price spike have no choice but to buy, and a gross price hike at that moment is a forced transfer to whoever is selling. The main honest objection is the vagueness of the standard — without a safe harbor for documented cost increases, some legitimate price increases could get swept in, and sellers might hesitate to bring extra supply into a shortage. That is a design question, not a reason the bill could not work; states with gouging laws have enforced them for years. On balance the bill helps ordinary people and its costs fall on sellers who raise prices abnormally during emergencies.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the last weeks of the Congress, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never taken up — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on November 10, 2022, with no cosponsors [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on November 11 it went to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce [S5].
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no report, and no vote, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1, S5].
The bill never received a floor vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers who profit from raising prices sharply during emergencies — fuel retailers, online sellers, and other essential-goods vendors — are better off, because the federal ban and FTC enforcement never came into being. Consumers in states with weak anti-gouging laws are left with the protections they had.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Democrat and drew no cosponsors from either party, so it never progressed far enough to reveal whether support or opposition split by party [S4].

industries.note: The bill specifically defines consumer fuel — gasoline, diesel, heating oil, propane, jet fuel — as an essential good, so gas stations and heating-fuel sellers could face FTC penalties for gross price spikes during declared emergencies or fuel shortages. Consumers have no alternative fuel source in those moments, so the industry's gain from price spikes is the public's loss.

industries.industry: Retailers and online sellers of essential goods
industries.note: Grocery chains, hardware stores, marketplace sellers, and hotels selling essentials would be exposed to FTC enforcement for unconscionably excessive pricing during disasters. This is the industry segment where gouging complaints — water, generators, masks, lodging — are most common.
The bill hands the FTC a new statutory price-gouging prohibition to enforce, with rulemaking authority, a public complaint hotline, and extended jurisdiction over common carriers and nonprofits.
